unit.title: Solving school problems in Python: timetables, routes, assignment

lesson.title: Exams without clashes
lesson.subtitle: A clash map, the fewest slots, and what fairness costs

video.title: Exams without clashes
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: A clash map and quick rules

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds an exam timetable with two exams circled in the same slot; a pupil eats lunch while writing.
scenes.animation: The two circled exams pulse red.
scenes.narration: Last year, a pupil found two of his exams in the same slot. He sat one of them in the staff room at lunchtime. This year I want no clashes, and as few slots as possible.

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: exams without clashes, as a picture and as a model.

scenes.visual: Eight dots appear; lines join dots that share a pupil; dots take colours.
scenes.animation: Lines draw between dots; colours fill in.
scenes.narration: Draw each exam as a dot. Join two dots when some pupil takes both exams: those two can’t share a slot. Now giving exams slots is colouring the dots, so that joined dots get different colours.

scenes.visual: Two columns: greedy colouring the map with four colours; DSatur with three.
scenes.animation: Each column colours its map dot by dot.
scenes.narration: A quick rule: go down the list, and give each exam the first slot with no clash. In the lab, that needs four slots. A smarter rule, DSatur, always does next the exam that is hardest to place, and needs three.

scenes.visual: Omar’s three exams form a triangle, each a different colour; a stamp ‘3 is the fewest’ lands.
scenes.animation: The triangle’s sides draw; the stamp drops.
scenes.narration: Can it be done in two? No. Omar’s three exams, maths, Arabic and French, all clash with each other, so they need three different slots. A group of exams that all clash is called a clique, and it proves that fewer is impossible.

scenes.visual: Code typed on a card, with the goal line highlighted.
scenes.animation: Code types itself line by line.
scenes.narration: In CP-SAT, each exam’s slot is a variable. For every pupil, their exams must all be in different slots. A variable called last is at least every slot, and the goal is to make it as small as possible.

scenes.visual: The phone prints OPTIMAL and slots used: 3; beside it, the greedy result 4 crossed out.
scenes.animation: Output types out; a check badge pops.
scenes.narration: The solver answers three, and says OPTIMAL. That word matters: the solver has proved that no plan with two slots exists, just as Omar’s clique said. A quick rule can only say “this works”; a solver can say “this is the best”.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah holds two cards: 4 slots and 3 slots OPTIMAL. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A quick rule found four slots, and the solver says OPTIMAL with three. What does the word OPTIMAL add?

scenes.visual: A clock shows three exams back to back for Omar; a second plan spreads them over five slots.
scenes.animation: The back-to-back exams squeeze; then they spread out.
scenes.narration: A proof: no plan with fewer slots exists. But look at Omar and Tarek: with three slots, they sit three exams back to back. Add the rule “no pupil sits exams in two slots in a row”, and the fewest becomes five. Fewer slots, or rested pupils: that’s a trade-off.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah with pupils and teachers around a table, two exam plans side by side.
scenes.animation: Hands point at both plans; one plan gets a tick.
scenes.narration: Who should decide that trade-off? Not the solver, and not one timetabler alone. Ask the pupils who sit the exams and the teachers who mark them, then write the agreed rule into the model.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: the clash map of eight exams, buttons below, a slot counter.
scenes.animation: A finger taps each button; dots change colour.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: Exam slots without clashes
scenes.narration: In the app, open “Exam slots without clashes”. Press Greedy, then DSatur, then “How few slots?”. Then untick Omar, and colour the map yourself.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma points at Tarek’s row: three exams in a row. Three answer cards appear.
scenes.on_screen_text: Three in a row for Tarek?
scenes.narration: Your turn. Our model says three slots, OPTIMAL, but Tarek has three exams back to back. What should we do?

scenes.visual: The answer card gets the check; four summary lines and a takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: Agree the rule with the people it affects, add it, solve again, and say openly what it costs. Remember: exams are dots, shared pupils are lines, and slots are colours. A clique proves the fewest. And OPTIMAL means best for the goal you wrote, not best for every pupil.

scenes.visual: Pupils on the playground with chalk dots and string lines between them, coloured caps on the dots.
scenes.animation: String stretches between dots; caps change colour.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: list next term’s exams, and let pupils draw the clash map with chalk or string. Colour it with as few slots as you can. Then ask: who has two exams in a row, and is that fair?

checkpoints.prompt: A quick rule found 4 slots; the solver says OPTIMAL with 3. What does OPTIMAL add?

options.text: That 3 is fewer than the quick rule found
That no plan with fewer slots exists
That 3 slots are fair to every pupil

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — OPTIMAL is a proof: no plan with 2 slots exists. Omar’s three clashing exams show why.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — beating the quick rule isn’t the point. OPTIMAL means the solver proved no plan with fewer slots exists.

checkpoints.prompt: Three slots is OPTIMAL, but Tarek has three exams back to back. What should we do?

options.text: Agree a fairness rule, add it, and solve again
Leave Tarek out of the model

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — OPTIMAL is best for the goal we wrote. Agree the fairness rule with pupils and teachers, add it, and see what it costs.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — OPTIMAL only means the fewest slots. Tarek’s day is a fairness question: agree a rule, add it, and solve again.
